title: Measurement and data health
hired_for: An owner hires this screen so every number they act on is right: no tracking gaps, platform and store numbers agree or the gap is explained, and each number shows how fresh it is.

jobs.job: Tell me each morning which numbers I can trust
jobs.why: Budgets move on yesterday's numbers. If a feed broke or a tag stopped firing, the owner acts on a wrong number and loses money before anyone notices.

watch.metric: pass, warn or fail grade for yesterday's data across every connected source, daily
watch.source: checks run on Shopify, GA4, Meta, Google Ads, Klaviyo and marketplace feeds

drives.metric: share of spend decisions made on data that passed the check

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: nobody checks, and a broken Meta feed showed zero sales for 2 days before budgets were cut. After: the check flags it by 9am and no budget moves on bad data.

jobs.job: Close the gap between what ad platforms claim and what the store sold
jobs.why: Meta, Google and TikTok each take credit for the same sales, so their totals add up to more than the store made. Scaling on claimed revenue burns cash.

watch.metric: platform-reported revenue divided by store-reported revenue for the same days: Meta plus Google Ads claimed purchase value against Shopify net sales, weekly
watch.source: Meta Ads Manager, Google Ads, Shopify

drives.metric: ad budget moved on store-confirmed sales

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: platforms claim $610,000 against $420,000 in store sales, a 1.45 ratio nobody explains. After: the gap is split by cause and budgets use the store number within 2 weeks.

jobs.job: Know where each order came from
jobs.why: If a large share of orders has no known source, the owner cannot tell which channel to grow. Each unknown order is a budget decision made blind.

watch.metric: share of store orders with a known source (tracked link, ad click id or survey answer), weekly
watch.source: Shopify orders with UTM and click id fields, GA4, post-purchase survey

drives.metric: share of revenue that can be credited to a channel

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: 38% of orders show as direct or unknown. After: link tags and a survey bring known source orders from 62% to 85% within 30 days.

jobs.job: Make sure every purchase gets tracked
jobs.why: When GA4 misses purchases, conversion rate, channel reports and funnel numbers are all wrong, and good channels look weak.

watch.metric: GA4 purchases divided by Shopify orders for the same dates, daily
watch.source: GA4 and Shopify

drives.metric: accuracy of channel and conversion reports

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: GA4 records 81% of store orders. After: the checkout tag and consent setup are fixed and GA4 records 95% within 7 days.

jobs.job: Make Meta see every sale once, and match it to a real person
jobs.why: Meta learns who to show ads to from purchase signals. Missed, doubled or poorly matched sales make it bid on the wrong people and raise cost per sale.

watch.metric: Meta event match quality score for Purchase (0 to 10) and duplicate purchase share, weekly
watch.source: Meta Events Manager

drives.metric: Meta cost per purchase

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: match quality is 5.1 and 9% of purchases count twice. After: browser and server events share one event id, match quality reaches 7.8, and doubles fall under 2% within 14 days.

jobs.job: Know how fresh each number is
jobs.why: A report that looks current may be 3 days old because a sync failed. The owner needs to see the age of a number next to the number.

watch.metric: hours since each source last synced against its expected schedule, live
watch.source: sync log for Shopify, GA4, Meta, Google Ads, Klaviyo and marketplace feeds

drives.metric: share of numbers read while stale

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: the Amazon feed has not synced in 52 hours and nothing says so. After: every number carries its age and stale sources are flagged within 1 hour.

jobs.job: Check tracking after every site or app change
jobs.why: A new theme, checkout app or consent banner can silently stop purchase or add to cart events. Every day it runs broken is a day of wrong reports.

watch.metric: count of key events (view product, add to cart, begin checkout, purchase) that dropped over 30% in the 24 hours after a site change
watch.source: GA4, Meta Events Manager, change log in the brand brain

drives.metric: days of broken tracking per quarter

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: a theme update broke add to cart tracking for 11 days. After: the check runs the day after each change and breaks are fixed within 24 hours.

jobs.job: Explain why a number moved before anyone reacts
jobs.why: When revenue drops, teams guess and change the wrong thing. Splitting the change into visits, buy rate and order size shows where to look first.

watch.metric: share of revenue swings over 10% split into sessions, conversion rate and order value within 24 hours
watch.source: Shopify and GA4

drives.metric: wrong fixes avoided per month

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: a 15% drop sets off a creative rebuild. After: the split shows sessions held and order value fell after a free shipping change, which is reversed in 2 days.

jobs.job: Ask buyers where they heard about us
jobs.why: Podcasts, word of mouth, creators and TV do not leave a click to track. A one-question survey after checkout shows the sources pixels cannot see.

watch.metric: share of orders with a survey answer and the top 5 answers, weekly
watch.source: Shopify post-purchase survey or Klaviyo

drives.metric: share of orders with a known source

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: no survey runs. After: 42% of buyers answer and podcasts show up as 12% of new customers, a channel no pixel credited.

jobs.job: Make Google Ads count only real purchases
jobs.why: Google Ads often counts add to carts, page views or duplicate purchases as sales, which inflates its return and misleads its bidding.

watch.metric: Google Ads purchase conversions divided by store orders from Google traffic, weekly, and whether purchase is the only main conversion
watch.source: Google Ads, Shopify, GA4

drives.metric: Google Ads cost per real purchase

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: Google Ads reports 1.6 conversions for every store order it drove. After: only purchase stays as a main conversion and the ratio is 1.05 within 7 days.

jobs.job: Spot a broken funnel step the day it breaks
jobs.why: A drop from cart to checkout can be a bug, a stock issue or a real change in shoppers. Comparing each step to the brand's own history catches it early.

watch.metric: conversion at each step (product view, add to cart, checkout, purchase) against the brand's own 90-day average, daily
watch.source: GA4 ecommerce events

drives.metric: store conversion rate

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: checkout to purchase fell from 52% to 41% for 4 days before anyone looked. After: the drop is flagged on day 1 and a payment app bug is fixed the same day.

jobs.job: Tag every link so each channel gets fair credit
jobs.why: Links without tracking tags show up as direct or unassigned, so email, creators and paid social look smaller than they are.

watch.metric: share of paid and email clicks that arrive with valid link tags, and share of sessions in direct or unassigned, weekly
watch.source: GA4 traffic acquisition

drives.metric: share of orders with a known source

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: 27% of sessions land in direct or unassigned. After: one tagging rule is applied to every link and that share falls to 12% within 14 days.

jobs.job: Keep test orders and our own visits out of the numbers
jobs.why: Staff visits, agency checks and test orders inflate traffic, lower conversion rate and add fake sales.

watch.metric: share of sessions from internal addresses and count of test orders in revenue, weekly
watch.source: GA4 internal traffic filter, Shopify orders

drives.metric: accuracy of conversion rate and revenue

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: 6% of sessions are staff and agencies, and 14 test orders sit in revenue. After: both are filtered out and conversion rate is restated within a day.

jobs.job: Audit the GA4 setup from end to end
jobs.why: Short data retention, wrong time zone, missing domains or wrong key events make every GA4 report quietly wrong.

watch.metric: share of critical GA4 setup checks passing (retention, domains, filters, key events, currency, time zone), weekly
watch.source: GA4 Admin settings

drives.metric: share of purchases GA4 records

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: 7 of 12 checks pass and data is kept for 2 months only. After: all 12 pass and history is kept for 14 months within a week.

jobs.job: Keep bots out of the numbers
jobs.why: Bot visits raise sessions, lower conversion rate and can make a good page or campaign look broken.

watch.metric: share of sessions flagged as bots against the brand's own baseline, and days when Shopify and GA4 sessions split by over 20%, daily
watch.source: GA4, Shopify sessions, Cloudflare or platform bot reports

drives.metric: accuracy of conversion rate

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: one day shows 18,000 extra sessions from a single city and conversion rate halves. After: the traffic is flagged as bots and excluded before anyone acts on it.

jobs.job: Send ad platforms the value of a sale that matters
jobs.why: When purchase events carry the wrong value, currency or include tax and shipping, the platforms optimise for the wrong customers.

watch.metric: share of purchase events sent with correct value, currency, product ids and a new or returning flag, weekly
watch.source: Meta Events Manager, Google Ads conversion diagnostics

drives.metric: cost per new customer

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: purchase value includes tax and shipping and no new customer flag is sent. After: value is net sales with a new customer flag and cost per new customer falls within 30 days.

jobs.job: Count new customers the same way everywhere
jobs.why: Meta, Google and the store each define new customer differently. Without one count, cost per new customer is a guess.

watch.metric: gap between platform-reported new customers and store first-time orders, weekly
watch.source: Shopify first-order flag, Meta and Google Ads new customer reports

drives.metric: cost per new customer from store data

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: Meta reports 1,900 new customers in a month and the store shows 1,150. After: the store count is the one number used and budgets reset against it.

jobs.job: Find out if a channel really adds sales
jobs.why: A channel can claim sales that would have happened anyway, like branded search or retargeting. A holdout test shows what it truly adds.

watch.metric: extra orders from a holdout test divided by the orders the platform claimed, per test
watch.source: Meta or Google Ads lift tests, geo holdout against Shopify orders

drives.metric: budget moved to channels that add sales

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: retargeting claims 900 orders a month. After: a 4 week holdout shows it adds 250, and $12,000 a month moves to prospecting.

jobs.job: Use one meaning for each number
jobs.why: When revenue means one thing in Shopify, another in the agency deck and another in the books, meetings turn into arguments about numbers instead of decisions.

watch.metric: count of key numbers with more than one definition in use
watch.source: metric definitions in the brand brain

drives.metric: time spent reconciling numbers each week

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: revenue has 3 definitions across reports. After: one written rule (net sales, tax out, returns counted) is used everywhere within 2 weeks.

jobs.job: Line up attribution windows across platforms
jobs.why: Meta counts a sale up to 7 days after a click and GA4 uses a different model. Comparing them without the same window leads to wrong budget moves.

watch.metric: gap between last click and platform credit per channel on the same window, weekly
watch.source: GA4 attribution reports, Meta and Google Ads

drives.metric: budget moved on like-for-like numbers

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: Meta shows 3.2x return and GA4 shows 1.1x for the same week. After: both are read on the same window with the gap labelled and explained.

jobs.job: Keep privacy consent from blinding the tracking
jobs.why: Consent banners set up wrong either block tracking for most visitors or fire tags before consent. One loses data, the other is a legal risk.

watch.metric: share of sessions with analytics consent granted and share of tags firing before consent, weekly
watch.source: GA4 consent reports, consent banner logs

drives.metric: share of purchases GA4 records

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: tags fire before consent on 3 pages and 30% of EU visits are lost. After: the banner is fixed and consent mode fills modelled data within a week.

jobs.job: Read repeat buying by cohort, not one blended rate
jobs.why: A blended returning customer rate hides whether newer customers come back less than older ones. Cohorts show it months earlier.

watch.metric: 90-day repeat purchase rate by first-order month, monthly
watch.source: Shopify orders by customer

drives.metric: accuracy of lifetime value estimates

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: returning rate is 31% and looks stable. After: cohorts show 90-day repeat fell from 18% to 12% for spring customers, so the welcome flow is fixed.

jobs.job: See AI assistant visits as their own source
jobs.why: Shoppers now arrive from ChatGPT, Perplexity and similar tools. Lumped into referral or direct, this growing source stays invisible.

watch.metric: sessions and orders from AI assistants, weekly
watch.source: GA4 with a custom channel group

drives.metric: share of orders with a known source

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: AI visits hide in referral. After: a custom channel shows 1,400 sessions and 60 orders a month from AI assistants.

jobs.job: Credit ads for the sales they drive on Amazon and in stores
jobs.why: Meta and TikTok ads also push sales on Amazon and at retail, which the store never sees. Without this, good ads get cut.

watch.metric: Amazon branded search volume and sales against weekly ad spend, and sales from tagged links to Amazon
watch.source: Amazon Brand Analytics, Amazon Attribution, Meta Ads Manager

drives.metric: total revenue credited to each channel

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: Meta is judged on store sales only. After: Amazon branded sales rise 20% in weeks of heavy Meta spend, and that lift is shown next to Meta.

jobs.job: Split budget across channels with a model that sees untracked ones
jobs.why: Click tracking misses TV, podcasts, creators and word of mouth. A model built on weekly spend and sales estimates what each channel adds.

watch.metric: modelled share of sales per channel against what each platform claims, monthly
watch.source: weekly Shopify sales and spend by channel

drives.metric: budget split across channels

jobs.now_after: Example: Now: no model exists. After: 2 years of weekly data show podcasts add more than their clicks show and Google brand search adds less.
